transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Elliot Morgan (CTO - Cascade), Samira Khan (Lead Eng), Ravi Patel (DevOps)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood. We also have Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick agenda — sdk walkthrough for Python/TS, auth and env setup, and then time for questions. Sound good?

[00:14] Elliot: Yep, sounds good. We're particularly interested in how quickly we can get the inference calls into our microservices, and what the auth flow looks like for our VPC/pilot.

[00:27] Priya: Cool. I'll share my screen in a sec. Just to set expectations, the Redwood SDKs are lightweight — Python and TypeScript — and we have quickstarts that cover streaming, batching, and embeddings. For Dedicated/Private we also support SAML-based SSO and customer-managed keys.

[00:45] Samira: When you say SAML, does that cover both Console access and API token issuance? We need RBAC for different teams.

[00:52] Priya: Yes, Console SSO is SAML/OIDC, and for API calls we can provision short-lived tokens tied to user identities via our private control plane in VPC mode. For hosted mode it's API key or mTLS. There's also integration with KMS/HSM for encryption at rest.

[01:10] Ravi: mTLS — interesting, we might prefer it for service-to-service. How do you rotate certificates?

[01:16] Priya: We support automated rotation via the private agent, or you can use your own certificate manager in the VPC deployment. We'll include the rotation docs in the quickstart.

[01:32] Jordan: Alright I'll pull up the Python quickstart on the repo now — //shared link//. This is a one-file example to do simple text generation: set REDWOOD_API_KEY environment variable, pip install redwood-sdk, then call Client.generate.

[01:50] Priya: Note — in the code we show two auth flows: 1) static API key in env for quick dev and 2) exchanging a SAML/OIDC assertion for a short-lived token in Private mode. The TypeScript flow is similar.

[02:05] Elliot: Can you show the TypeScript snippet too? Our edge services are Node-based.

[02:11] Priya: Sure, quick paste. import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'... const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); Then client.chat.stream(...) for streaming responses. We also demo an SDK helper for incremental decoding so you can pipe tokens to the user UI with low latency.

[02:33] Samira: Latency — what's the typical p95 for hosted vs dedicated? We're sensitive to sub-200ms for short prompts.

[02:40] Jordan: For small prompts and small-ish open models, hosted p95 can be around 150–250ms depending on region and model. Dedicated gives more consistent p95 — often under 120–180ms for the same workload because you get reserved GPUs and reduced cold-starts.

[02:57] Ravi: And cost delta between hosted and dedicated? We have to justify committed spend.

[03:03] Jordan: Dedicated is commit-based, you pay for reserved capacity but get predictable per-token cost which tends to be lower at scale. We can run an expected usage calculation once we know your token volumes — we'll include a cost estimate in the follow-up.

[03:20] Priya: Back to the quickstart, here's the env file example: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxxx OR for Private: REDWOOD_PRIVATE_HOST=https://private.cascade.redwood.local; REDWOOD_CLIENT_CERT=/path/to/cert. Then Dockerfile example to run in your staging cluster.

[03:38] [Screen share shows code and console logs]

[03:52] Priya: I'm going to run a sample chat so you can see streaming. Note: real transcripts sometimes show quirks, uh tokenization differences across model variants.

[04:05] [04:05] Priya: (typing) client.chat.stream({ model: 'rw-large-v1', input: 'Summarize the latest order activity for user 12345' })

[04:18] [04:18] Console output: streaming tokens appear — "Recent orders include..."

[04:30] Elliot: Looks good. Quick question — for embeddings we plan to re-index nightly, do you recommend running embedding calls through the same SDK or a separate batch job?

[04:40] Priya: Either works. We have an embeddings client optimized for bulk calls with automatic retry/backoff. For large batch jobs we suggest dedicated compute pools or a background worker calling the SDK with batching enabled (we provide helpers for chunking).

[04:56] Samira: You mentioned caching and KV cache earlier in the doc — how does that interact with the SDK?

[05:02] Priya: The runtime maintains KV cache for transformer attention state on the server side; the SDK exposes a cache key mechanism so repetitive prefixes can be hit from cache. This reduces token compute for multi-turn conversations. It's automatic but you can control TTL via headers.

[05:20] Ravi: For PII, do you redact before sending? We need to guarantee no customer PII leaves our network for hosted mode.

[05:27] Jordan: That's a common constraint. For Private/VPC you can keep data in your network and use the on-prem agent so no raw payloads go to hosted. For hosted, we offer data residency options and can sign a DPA, but we usually recommend Private for strict PII rules. We'll attach the security questionnaire.

[05:47] Elliot: Great. Onboarding timeline — if we opt for a POC next week, what's realistic for us to get a benchmark?

[05:54] Priya: If you can provide a representative prompt set and staging VPC access, we can run a 2–3 day benchmark with typical concurrency. We'll validate latency, throughput, and cost. Prep time mainly depends on test data availability and VPC access, so the earlier you can share that the quicker we can start.

[06:13] Samira: We can spin up a staging namespace and give Priya a service account with limited scope. I'll coordinate with Ravi.

[06:20] Ravi: Yeah I'll put that together.

[06:25] Jordan: Cool, we also wanted to show the Console quickstart — the per-route dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns. I'll flip to the Console — apologies if the names are a bit off in the transcript, sometimes the auto-captions change Redwood Console to Redwood Consul.

[06:42] [Screen shows console dashboards]

[06:48] Jordan: Here's the model catalog, you can pin a model version for rollout, and set canary percentages. There's a Quickstart button which auto-generates the SDK config for Python or TS.

[07:03] Elliot: Nice. Can we integrate this with our SSO providers?

[07:07] Jordan: Yes, SAML/OIDC supported, and we have SCIM provisioning for user management for Private deployments.

[07:15] Samira: Any gotchas with our infra — we're on AWS in eu-west-1, using EKS and a Transit Gateway to customer data centers.

[07:24] Priya: Common setup. For Private we can deploy an on-prem agent in your VPC or run in your EKS cluster. Network egress rules for the agent are documented; for Dedicated you'll also want peering between our subnets and yours, or use private link depending on region. We'll add the network diagram to the follow-up.

[07:44] Elliot: One more — model quantization. We do care about cost but not at the expense of hallucinatory behaviour. How do you recommend balancing quantization and quality?

[07:55] Priya: Good call. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles by workload. For chat where accuracy is critical, we start with 8-bit quant, run eval sets against your prompt corpus, and only move to more aggressive quant if quality regressions are within your threshold. We tie regressions to eval sets so you can measure.

[08:18] Ravi: Do you do automated A/B rollouts in the Console for quantized vs full models?

[08:22] Jordan: Yes, canary rollouts by route/model with automatic fallback if error/latency thresholds tripped. We'll demo that in the POC.

[08:34] [08:34] Priya: Quick note about the SDK packaging: Python package is redwood-inference on PyPI, TS package is @redwood/inference on npm. The sample repo has a mono-repo with examples: streaming chat, embeddings batch, and a small microservice that demonstrates exponential backoff and idempotency for retries.

[08:55] Samira: Idempotency keys — important. Do you store request logs? We need audit logs for compliance.

[09:02] Priya: Yes, audit logs are part of the Console — request-level metadata, user attribution, and model versions. For Private deployments you can ship logs to your SIEM; for hosted we retain per the plan. We'll include retention options in the security doc.

[09:20] Elliot: Ok this is all very helpful. Anything else we should watch out for during integration?

[09:25] Jordan: Mostly: share representative prompt set, staging access, and decide preferred auth (short-lived tokens via SAML or API keys for quick POC). We'll prepare the quickstart with both flows.

[09:38] Samira: Sounds good. We'll aim to get the staging VPC access to Priya by Monday.

[09:44] [Cross talk: logistics and emails]

[09:52] Jordan: Alright, quick recap: Jordan to send SDK quickstart repo, Priya to draft benchmark plan and test dataset instructions, Samira to provide staging access; we'll schedule the POC next week. We'll also send SOC2 and security questionnaire. Any final Qs?

[10:10] Elliot: No more from me. Thanks everyone.

[10:15] Jordan: Thank you all — we'll follow up with the links and a calendar invite for the POC kickoff.

[10:22] End of recording.
